title: English — Grade 9 Scholarship (IGCSE Paper 1 Reading)

instructions:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500), Paper 1 Reading — 2 hours.

- Answer **all** questions.
- Write your answer to each question in the space provided.
- Dictionaries are **not** allowed.
- The number of marks for each question or part question is shown in brackets [ ].
- The reading texts are provided with each section.

sections.title: Question 1(a)–(e): Text A, Bees
sections.instructions: Read Text A, *Bees*, and then answer Questions 1(a)–(e). (In the original paper the text is printed with line numbers; the phrases referred to by line number are quoted in the questions.)
sections.passage:
**Text A: Bees**

A bee colony is populated by a queen, about 200 male drones and thousands of underdeveloped female workers. The queen is the largest member of the colony due to the workers having fed her a special diet.

The queen is the mother of all the workers and also the male drones in the hive. She remains inside, attended by the workers who groom and feed her. The sole purpose of the drone is to mate with her so that the hive continues.

Bees have different characteristics that make them suited to pollinating certain plants. For example, the early bumblebee's small size and agility allow it to enter plants with drooping flowers. The larger garden bumblebee is better at pollinating the deep flowers because its longer tongue can reach deep inside them.

Plants can only grow because of pollination. Bees' transference of pollen between flowering plants enables a plant to reproduce and produce food. The cycle of a plant's life keeps turning in this way.

So thanks to these small creatures, we enjoy a range of foods from orchard fruits to coffee and vanilla. And if you are wearing cotton, that's because a cotton plant was pollinated. Maybe in your lessons at school you have come across bees too. This would be because many poets, artists, authors and scientists have found them a fascinating subject to study.

But bees are in trouble. Nowadays, many of us are aware of how human decisions impact on bee populations. A few organisations try to educate the public on how the pesticides we use on crops to make our food safer and more prolific are toxic to bees, damaging their mental capacities and ability to reproduce. Bee habitats, such as ponds, trees and flowers, are wiped out by our need to urbanise and build houses and by intensive farming methods. We really need to ask ourselves how much our thoughtlessness and selfishness might be costing us all.

sections.title: Question 1(f): Text B, Beekeeping
sections.instructions: Read Text B, *Beekeeping*, and then answer Question 1(f).
sections.passage:
**Text B: Beekeeping**

*This text is advice given by a practising beekeeper to other people considering keeping bees.*

Why be a beekeeper? Is it because you like honey? Want to help with local pollination? Aid the global honeybee crisis? Beekeeping is hard work and a considerable responsibility, so needs a lot of thought.

Actually, you may have no choice in the matter if beekeeping is forbidden in your area. My town requires hive registrations. You might just live somewhere where there are no restrictions on beekeeping, but that would be lucky.

Okay, so you are allowed to keep bees. It took me a while to receive a reply to my request for help from the online beekeeping organisation I contacted, presumably because the beekeepers were all out and about pursuing their hobby. In the end I discovered that there was a lot of advice out there, which I sifted through, finding some of it anecdotal and specific to certain circumstances rather than of use to me.

Naturally, I assumed that my spacesuit-like body and head protection would shield me from stings. Choosing clothing that is effective in keeping an angry swarm at bay is important, but bear in mind there is always the occasional unavoidable sting. Yes, it's happened to me even in a full beekeeping suit with gloves.

My bees fly up to eight kilometres when out foraging for nectar and pollen, and that's fine as I live in a rural area. Your urban neighbours may not be so happy about you keeping beehives in your back garden while they are out enjoying the sun.

And that brings me onto another matter. I have a field for my hives. They should be placed on a level site, receive sun during the day and be sheltered from strong winds, as well as being easily accessible for you and their stripy occupants.

In the beginning, I bought a heavy hive, intending to give my bees a robust and safe home. By harvest time, when the hives were full of honey, my aching back taught me I needed to purchase a lighter construction. Still now, I need a trusted friend (a fellow beekeeper) to help me shift those hives around.

The same friend and I have a reciprocal arrangement to look after our bees when either of us goes away. Bees can't be left for long periods. Hiring someone else to look after your bees can be costly and you need to be sure that person knows what they're doing.

I spent a lot of money getting started and I made a few expensive purchasing errors, from heavy hives to beekeeping accessories that I never actually used.

questions.prompt: Which bee is the biggest in a colony, according to paragraph 1?

**Using your own words**, explain what the text means by:

'special diet' (line 3)
questions.criteria:
1 mark for explaining 'special' in own words: particular / unusual / different from the others / specific to the queen.
1 mark for explaining 'diet' in own words: the food she is given / what she is fed / her feeding regime.
No marks for simply repeating the words 'special' or 'diet'.

questions.prompt:
**Using your own words**, explain what the text means by:

'sole purpose' (line 5).
questions.criteria:
1 mark for explaining 'sole' in own words: only / single / one and only.
1 mark for explaining 'purpose' in own words: reason for existing / function / job / role (the drone exists only to mate with the queen).
No marks for simply repeating the words 'sole' or 'purpose'.

questions.prompt:
Re-read paragraph 3 ('Bees have different ... deep inside them.').

Give **two** characteristics that make the early bumblebee and the garden bumblebee different.

Re-read paragraphs 4 and 5 ('Plants can ... subject to study.').

Identify **two** ways in which bee pollination is needed for plants.

Re-read paragraphs 4 and 5 ('Plants can ... subject to study.').

Explain how humans have benefited from the existence of bees.

Re-read paragraph 6 ('But bees ... costing us all.').

Why might some humans disregard the threats to bees?

According to Text B, what should people consider and do before taking up beekeeping?

You must **use continuous writing** (not note form) and **use your own words** as far as possible.

Your summary should not be more than 120 words.

**Up to 10 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 5 marks for the quality of your writing.**
questions.criteria:
Content (up to 10 marks, 1 per distinct point from Text B): beekeeping is hard work and a big responsibility, needing thought; check whether beekeeping is allowed locally / whether hives must be registered; seek advice and sift it, as some is anecdotal or not applicable; get effective protective clothing but accept the occasional unavoidable sting; consider neighbours — bees forage up to 8 km, urban neighbours may object; place hives on a level, sunny, wind-sheltered, easily accessible site; choose a lighter hive, as heavy ones are hard to move when full of honey; arrange for a trusted, knowledgeable person to care for the bees when away (bees can't be left long; hired help is costly); budget carefully — starting is expensive and purchasing mistakes are easy.
Writing (up to 5 marks): continuous prose, own words, well organised, concise, clear and accurate English.
Apply the 120-word limit: content beyond it should not earn credit.
